newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Canadian debut novel scores success abroad.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Canadian debut novel scores success abroad.

text.p: When Ann-Marie MacDonald began writing "Fall on Your Knees," she had the feeling her story of a tragic Atlantic-Canadian family would end up as a bad play.

Instead, it grew to become one of the most successful Canadian debut novels of recent years, earning bestseller status in Canada and critical acclaim abroad, including the top prize for new fiction in a British Commonwealth country.

Success began for MacDonald when she realised the story of "Fall on Your Knees," set mostly on Canada's remote Cape Breton Island, was far too ambitious to find life on the stage. "It was as though I had set out in my kitchen to bake one loaf of bread and this dough kept rising and rising until it was coming out the windows," she told Reuters.

The epic novel, which follows four generations of a family beset by incest, violence and early death, was a success even before hitting bookstores. Foreign rights were reported to have sparked a bidding war and earned "high five-figure" advances, a rarity for a Canadian novel. The book has since been published in Britain, Germany, the United States, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain.

Critics compare "Fall on Your Knees" with such successful literary debuts as E. Annie Proulx's Pulitizer Prize-winning "The Shipping News." The praise culminated in April when MacDonald won the Commonwealth Writers best first book award, given to a writer from one of the 53 Commonwealth countries.
Awards are nothing new for the 38-year-old Toronto resident. Before publishing "Fall On Your Knees" she was best known as a successful actress and playwright.

Her play "Goodnight Desdemona (Good Morning Juliet)" won Canada's top prize for drama in 1990 and has had more than 40 productions worldwide. MacDonald also has won Canadian prizes for television and film acting.

"Fall on Your Knees" came to life in her mind as a play, but a few weeks into its writing she decided something was very wrong. "I came to think that I must be writing a very bad play because the stage directions seemed to be getting out of hand and the monologues were just uncontrollable," she said.

When she realised the story had to be told as a novel, she felt equal parts excitement and terror. The process of writing the novel, which MacDonald called "the biggest acting job of my life," took five years.

The inspiration for "Fall on Your Knees" came partly from MacDonald's links to Cape Breton, a rugged east coast island with a history of hardship and poverty. Both her parents grew up there and MacDonald said the place has always haunted her.

Growing up hearing the tales and folklore of the island helped her conceive the story of the half-Scottish, half-Lebanese Piper family. The book follows their lives across two continents over 50 years, with much of the book set in Cape Breton and New York during the jazz age.

A couple of years into writing the novel, MacDonald said, she had inklings that she was creating a world readers would want to enter. The book's success has felt to her like the natural conclusion to years of effort.
"I tried to write the kind of book that I would want to read. And when I open a novel I'm just longing to be taken somewhere," she said.

MacDonald said her greatest satisfaction came not from awards or royalties but from her encounters with individual readers. Because of her background in film and theatre, she said, her goal was to reach as wide an audience -- to "invite as many people to the table" -- as possible.

She said she will now spend most of her time writing novels but vary the long hours with an occasional acting or theatre project. But she admitted to being daunted by the prospect of starting a new novel because of the expectations raised by the success of "Fall on Your Knees."
"It's scarier this time because apparently I know something about how to write a novel," she said, adding: "I don't really feel like I know much at all."
